disp-quote.p: The antibody studies need to be improved: The antibody, made against synthetic peptide within Human PACAP-38, is a polyclonal recognizing mammals; mouse human and rat. There is no evidence that zebrafish have the specific PACAP-38 protein (or at least the authors have omitted these references), nor that the antibody works in zebrafish. Many antibodies made in mammals do not work in zebrafish, thus one has to be very careful.

body.p: Positive control: The isotype controls are used to determine the background due to nonspecific antibody binding, but are not used to distinguish positive from negative cells. If there is no zebrafish protein available they should pre-absorb with the human protein.

Thank you for this concern as indeed many antibodies do not cross-react. PACAP-38 indeed exists in all teleost fish including zebrafish. Teleost fish express two PACAPs (PACAP1, encoded by the adcyap1a gene, and PACAP2, encoded by the adcyap1b gene). The zebrafish PACAP-38 sequence accession numbers are NM_152885.2 and NM_214715 for 1a and 1b, respectively. The % identity between human PACAP-38 and zebrafish PACAP-38 aminoacid sequences is very high (84.2%).
When looking at the amino acid sequence of the region recognized by the polyclonal antibody we used in our experiments, the conservation of that region is even higher (%).

To further ascertain the validity of the antibody staining performed, we conducted pre-adsorption experiments as suggested by the reviewer. Pre-absorption was performed with Clarias gariepinus PACAP-38 Sequence (N to C): HSDGIFTDSYSRYRKQMAVKKYLAAVLGRRYRQRFRNK which is almost identical to Danio rerio PACAP-38 (adcyap1a) Sequence N to C:
HSDGVFTDSYSRYRKQMAVKKYLATVLGKRYRQRYRSK (bolded letters of the only 4 amino acids that differ between both sequences).

The C. gariepinus PACAP-38 peptide has been extensively used in a variety of fish immunology studies (see for example doi: 10.3389/fimmu.2019.00926) due to the extremely high conservation of PACAP-38 across vertebrate phylogeny.

The new staining is shown in supplemental figure 11. In addition, we have attempted to clarify our exact methods in the text here “The rabbit isotype control for the PACAP-38 antibody showed no immunoreactivity within the glomeruli layers of the zebrafish OB.” and within the results.

disp-quote.p: Authors need to refer to the antibody staining as "PACAP-38-like"

body.p: Given the clear identification of PACAP in zebrafish as a direct ortholog of mammalian PACAP, we believe that identification of the immunofluorescence staining as “PACAP-38-like” would be incorrect. If anything, the most appropriate would be to label it as PACAP1 as previously used in the zebrafish literature (https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2019.00227) but we believe our revised manuscript clearly states that we are measuring PACAP1.

disp-quote.p: (2) "However, immune responses in the OB caused by pathogen332 detection or damage in the olfactory periphery without translocation into the brain are not well 333 understood."

body.p: Thank you for this deep reading of our paper and previous work. Our data do not address only crypt cells, and the assumption that our use of OSN is in fact referring to crypt cells is incorrect. While we have added background on crypt cells to the paper, we want to ensure that it is clear that we are using the term OSN to refer to any olfactory sensory neurons, not solely to crypt cells. In fact, our data indicate that OSNs beyond crypt cells are involved in responding to IHNV, mainly because multiple glomeruli (and not just the single glomerulus to which crypt cells project) are activated by viral administration.

We would like to point the reviewer to Schmidt et al., 2013, “Neurogenesis in zebrafish – from embryo to adult” which we have cited and used as a source to identify markers for neuronal progenitors in our single-cell dataset. This identification, combined with the fact that these clusters are the only ones which express PACAP1 (adcyap1a) serves as the evidence to support this claim.

Other comments:

(1) Are there any similarities or differences in how the zebrafish and rainbow trout OB neurons respond to the IHNV virus? For example, can the author compare the scRNA-seq data and rainbow trout transcriptomic data? Does the adcyap1a response also appear in rainbow trout?

body.p: Thus far, there is no comparable transcriptional data set for the rainbow trout OB. Importantly, both models are very different as IHNV is a disease of rainbow trout and replicates at low temperatures. As such, this live attenuated version of IHNV when delivered IN, is detected in the trout OE for 4 days (Larragoite et al, 2016) whereas in zebrafish the virus cannot be detected by 1 day.

disp-quote.p: (2) The behavioral response to viral stimulation is quite confusing. Theoretically, the zebrafish will increase their swimming speed to escape potentially harmful stimuli. The author concludes that the reduced swimming speed is due to the sickness of the zebrafish. Is there any inflammation/IFN response following virus infection?

body.p: The reviewer is correct that we expected to see increased escape behavior at the early, 15 m time point which we did not find. The decreased speed of the 1 d after I.N. IHNV compared to medium control animals is interesting and begs further investigation to elucidate. In order to see if there is inflammation, we used transgenic reporters of NF-kb to assess if there is increased activation of this element 1 day after IN virus delivery. It is possible that inflammation in the OB may suggest a reason for the sickness, lethargic behavior. However, we did not see an increase in fluorescence in the olfactory bulb of the NFkB reporter after intranasal administration of IHNV. Of course, we did not look at regions canonically involved in sickness behaviors such as the hypothalamus or the telencephalon. Thus, form our work we can only conclude that no NFkb activation occurs in the OB following IN viral delivery but the behavioral changes observed could be associated with inflammation in other areas of the brain. This wording has been added to the discussion of the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: For the larvae experiment, exposure the virus for 30 seconds may be hard to trigger the sick response. Do zebrafish only respond to live viruses? A more comprehensive behavior test that lasts longer time will be helpful to understand better how IHNV affects behavior.

body.p: Zebrafish larvae are a very different model than adult animals. Behaviors of larvae are more deeply investigated in the literature, and direct comparisons between larval and adult behaviors cannot be made with our current understanding of zebrafish behavior. Here we only tested for rapid changes to larvae after virus response, because development of the animal over a day would likely be too confounding. We did see a decrease in speed in larvae immediately after virus administration to the arena. For larvae, decreased speed may not necessarily mean the same thing as in adults, but literature suggests that a decrease in speed at that developmental time point is likely an indicator of stress or anxiety. Further, our model virus is live, however attenuated. Perhaps the loss of pathogenicity has dampened behavioral responses we may otherwise observe from full-strength viruses. Overall, we agree that our behavioral changes are small, and lend themselves to more questions than answers. Future studies will certainly be aimed at looking more closely at the connection between the viral exposure in the nose and vertebrate animal behavior changes.

disp-quote.p: (3) For the OB calcium imaging, it is unclear why the positive control KCl did not increase OB neuron calcium. What is the percentage of the OB neuron that can be activated? Are these IHNV-responsive OB neurons located in a designated OB region?

body.p: Thank you for this comment. We have replaced the KCl control in figure 2 with an amino acid odorant control, and we have also included images indicating the location of these IHNV-responsive neurons.

disp-quote.p: (4) The sc-RNA sequencing data generated in this paper can be quite helpful for the field. Is this dataset generated from adult zebrafish? If so, can the authors clarify this in the figure legend and method? Better annotation to assign the neuronal, microglia, and oligodendrocyte subgroup function/feature will be helpful. In addition, if the author can provide evidence to validate some of the markers identified in this dataset will also be helpful.

body.p: Thank you, indeed we are excited that others can use it as a resource. We have updated the figure legend and methods stating that this was done in adult zebrafish. We agree that validation of cell types would be helpful for understanding cellular interactions within the OB after viral delivery. However, such in-depth analysis and imaging was outside the scope of this project and its resources. We diligently reviewed available literature for the proposed cell identities within the text. Because we did not further validate these cell identities with other techniques, we used broad cluster names at the resolution that the literature was exceptionally clear on. For example, oligodendrocytes express olig 1 and olig 2, but the functional difference in our two clusters was not investigated here. It is the authors’ hope that this data set will be helpful to other olfactory bulb researchers, and that over time these assignments can be fully validated.

disp-quote.p: (5) The results that IHNV induces the adcyap1a+ OB neuronal cell cluster are very interesting. In the discussion, the author mentioned that the adcyap1a+ OB neuron cluster likely be the progenitor-like neurons. Are those neurons Edu+? Any lineage tracing evidence?

body.p: We agree, these are some of the most interesting findings in this study. We have not undertaken lineage tracing experiments for EdU-positive cells after I.N. IHNV or for PACAP/adcyap1a+ neurons because we do not currently have transgenic tools to follow these cells in a spatiotemporal way (i.e. a CreERT2 under adcyap1a or gap43). We believe that clusters assigned as Neuron 4 and 5 are progenitor or intermediate neuronal progenitors like based on their transcriptional profiles detailed in figures 4 and supplemental 2.
